newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Grow Biz steps up pace of store openings.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Grow Biz steps up pace of store openings.

text.p: Grow Biz International Inc, which franchises stores that sell used and new consumer items, said Friday more of its revenues will come from franchise fees and royalties in 1997 as it steps up the pace of store openings.

"We're looking to open between 240 and 300 stores in 1997, so we'll see a slight increase in franchise fees," Ronald Olson, president and chief executive officer of Grow Biz, said in a telephone interview.
By comparison, 253 stores opened in 1996 and 229 in 1995.

The company's revenue base has three components: the buying group, which arranges for the purchase of lower-cost new merchandise that is sold to franchisees at a small mark-up; franchise fees, which range from $100,000 to $180,000 per store; and royalties of three percent to five percent, based on weekly sales.

"I think next year that we're going to continue to see that (revenues from) our buying group is flat compared to a year ago," Olson said, "and our royalty stream will continue to be 30 percent higher than in 1996."
Grow Biz has five chains: Play It Again Sports, Once Upon a Child, Computer Renaissance, Disc Go Round and Music Go Round.

The company currently has more than 1,000 stores in North America, with another 379 franchises awarded. Profit margins for the stores, according to Olson, range from between 40 percent for Computer Renaissance to 56 percent for Once Upon a Child.
"We have a backlog of about 350 stores that have been sold but haven't opened," Olson said, "so we will see the revenue stream from royalties increase once those stores open."

Olson said Grow Biz launched a strategy in late 1995 where more franchisees bought goods directly from vendors. That lowered revenues for the company's buying group by 24 percent in the fourth quarter, but Olson said other factors compensated for the decline.

"Our gross margins were up, our expense controls increased and we've finally built the infrastructure, the buildings, the equipment," Olson said. "Now we're expecting to see the synergies of having all of our systems in place."

Grow Biz reported total revenue of $21.6 million in the 1996 third quarter, down 14 percent from $25.1 million in the same period in 1995. However, net income reached $887,800, a 52-percent improvement from the $583,900 reported in the third quarter of 1995.

Olson said the primary customers for nearly all of the store concepts are mothers with small children, especially those with kids who need sports equipment, are outgrowing their clothes, need access to a computer at home or are looking for a musical instrument to learn to play.
